implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library supplies the lexing half: StringScanner (strscan) keeps a scan pointer and offers scan/check/skip/unscan plus pos, which are exactly the token-consumption primitives a recursive-descent parser needs, so a parser is a class with one method per rule calling scan or check and raising a positioned ParseError on mismatch - tokens need never be materialised as objects. What replaces the classic structure is StringScanner plus Ruby's own style (methods, hashes, exceptions instead of token classes and tables); Ruby's new parser, Prism, is likewise hand-written, and its design document describes the error-tolerant hand-written approach. Keep this form for small grammars and tooling; reach for a generator (racc) or the parser gem only when the grammar is large.
code_sketch:
require 'strscan'
class Parser
  def initialize(src) = @s = StringScanner.new(src)
  def expr                                 # one method per rule
    left = term
    while @s.check(/[+-]/)                 # lookahead without consuming
      left = [:binary, @s.scan(/[+-]/), left, term]   # loop, not left recursion
    end
    left
  end
  def term = @s.scan(/\d+/)&.to_i || raise("expected number at #{@s.pos}")
end
pitfalls: StringScanner#scan returns nil on failure, so a rule that ignores the nil check silently parses nothing and returns a wrong tree; wrap mandatory matches in a helper that raises with @s.pos.
Regexp scanning backtracks: a pathological pattern (nested quantifiers) over untrusted input can take exponential time, so keep patterns anchored and simple.
StringScanner holds a reference to its source string and one scanner per parse is the safe rule; reusing a scanner across inputs or unscan-ing past a failed alternative produces subtle pointer bugs.
